rationale: David prepares a tent for the ark in Chronicles; Samuel describes the ark being placed inside the tent David had pitched, completing that preparation.
The prepared tent for the ark in David’s city is recalled when the later account explains that David had brought the ark to a tent he prepared in Jerusalem, distinguishing it from the tent at Gabaon.
David restricts carrying the ark and perpetual ministry to the Levites because the Lord chose them; Deuteronomy explicitly sets Levi apart to bear the covenant ark and minister before the Lord.

David reserves carrying the ark to the Levites; Numbers assigns carrying the covered holy objects to Kohath’s sons and forbids touching them on pain of death, providing a specific transport rule behind that concern.
Both assemblies of all Israel are organized to bring up God’s ark; chapter 15 specifies Jerusalem and the prepared destination after the earlier procession’s interruption.
The assembled people bring the ark to David’s prepared place, and the next chapter records it actually being set in the middle of his pitched tent.
The gathering of Aaron’s sons and the Levites supplies the priestly and Levitical personnel whom David orders to purify themselves and who then do so for the ark’s ascent.
Ouriel heads the Kaathite group of one hundred twenty; David subsequently summons Ouriel among the Levite rulers and charges those ancestral-house leaders with purification and bringing up the ark.

The Merari family assembled under Asaia belongs to the Levitical service structure for which Moses assigned four wagons and eight oxen. The connection is the family’s ministry, not an equation of these numbered groups or transport occasions.
Joel leads the one hundred fifty from Gersam’s sons and is subsequently named among the summoned Levite rulers charged to purify themselves and bring up the ark.

The two hundred from Elisaphan’s sons, led by Samaias, constitute a named component of the immediately introduced assembly of Aaron’s sons and the Levites; the heading explains this group’s place in the procession roster.

The procession includes a group from Hebron’s sons under Eliel; the earlier genealogy lists Hebron among Kaath’s sons, supplying the named ancestral branch rather than identifying an individual by a similar name.

The group from Oziel’s sons under Amminadab belongs to a branch named in the earlier genealogy, where Oziel is listed among Kaath’s sons; the passages concern the branch and its later assembled descendants.
The summoned priests and six Levite rulers are the immediate recipients of David’s command to purify themselves for carrying the ark, followed by the priests’ and Levites’ compliance.

David requires the Levite rulers and their brethren to purify themselves before bringing up the ark; Numbers explicitly orders the Levites’ purification and gives its rites. Chronicles does not enumerate those rites here.

David’s recollection that God cut among them after the earlier failure recalls Oza’s touching the ark, death, and the named Cutting of Oza. The present explanation adds the failure to seek according to judgment.

David interprets the earlier breach as failure to seek according to judgment; Numbers supplies the specific rule that the appointed bearers must not touch the holy objects lest they die, illuminating the ark-handling failure narrated in chapter 13.

The priests and Levites purify themselves before bringing up the ark; Numbers supplies the earlier command to purify the Levites. The present notice does not specify which purification procedures were performed.
Chronicles explicitly attributes carrying the ark with poles to Moses’ written command; Exodus orders poles through the ark’s rings for carrying it and requires them to remain there.
The Levites carry the ark with poles under Moses’ command; Numbers withholds wagons from Kohath’s sons because their sanctuary burdens must be borne on their shoulders.
David orders singers with harps, lyres, and cymbals; the subsequent assignments distribute those three instrument types among named musicians, detailing the implementation of his instruction.
David’s command to appoint instrumental singers for the ark corresponds to the earlier account of his appointment of singers whose ministry before the tent continued until Solomon built the house.
Aiman, Asaph, and Aithan are appointed as the principal singers, and the later instrument assignment explicitly names the same three to sound bronze cymbals.

The second-rank brethren are introduced as being with the singers just appointed under David’s instruction; the preceding commission and named leaders establish the grammatical scope of this continuing personnel list.
The three cymbal players Aiman, Asaph, and Aithan are the three singers named in the appointment, connecting their specific instrument duty to the preceding choice of leaders.
The named group’s harps according to Alaimoth implement one of the instrument categories David commanded for the singers. The connection does not assign an unattested meaning to Alaimoth.
The named group’s lyres implement David’s command to appoint singers with lyres among their instruments. Amasenith is preserved as the source’s designation without an inferred musical definition.

Chonenia’s discerning leadership of the songs belongs to the organized singing ministry David commissions through the Levite rulers; this specifies oversight of the performance rather than identifying him with an unrelated similarly named person.

Barachia and Elkana are assigned as gatekeepers of the ark; the earlier gatekeeper description identifies guarding the Lord’s tent-house as the duty of that service. It does not identify these two with a different roster.

The named priests sound trumpets before God’s ark, corresponding to Numbers’ assignment of trumpet blowing to Aaron’s sons, the priests; the ark gatekeepers remain a separate duty within the source verse.

The trumpets sounded before the ark stand within the joyous procession and its sacrifices; Numbers specifically commands trumpet sounding on days of gladness over burnt offerings and sacrifices of deliverance.

Both accounts describe David bringing the ark from the house where it had stayed to his city with gladness. Chronicles names Abdedom and adds elders and commanders; Samuel names Obed-edom and gives the report of blessing.

The resumed ascent from Abdedom’s house follows the earlier interruption in which the ark stayed three months in the house named Abeddara and God blessed Abeddaram. All three source forms remain distinct within the consecutive ark narrative.

Both procession accounts associate carrying the ark with sacrifice. Chronicles attributes strength to God and specifies seven calves and seven rams; Samuel speaks of seven dancing companies and a calf and a lamb, without equating those details.

Both accounts describe David’s robe during the ark procession. Chronicles specifies fine linen and includes the Levites, singers, and their leader; Samuel describes a distinctive robe and David’s instrumental playing.

Both accounts bring the ark up with Israel and audible celebration. Samuel names shouting and a trumpet; Chronicles gives signals, sopher, trumpets, cymbals, harps, and lyres, retaining the fuller instrumentation.
Both ark processions feature David or Israel making music with lyres, harps, cymbals, and trumpets; the earlier list also includes tambourines, while the later verse adds signals and sopher.

At the ark’s arrival in David’s city, Saul’s daughter watches David dancing and playing through a window and despises him inwardly. The accounts use Melchol and Michal respectively and soul versus heart.
The inward contempt at the window is developed in Samuel’s later exchange: Saul’s daughter criticizes David’s public conduct, and David explains his celebration before the Lord who chose him.

Both accounts place the ark in the tent David pitched and join that placement to whole burnt offerings and a second offering category, called offerings of deliverance in Chronicles and peace offerings in Samuel.
The ark’s placement in the tent completes David’s earlier preparation of a place and tent for it in his city.
David’s blessing of the people in the Lord’s name follows his completion of the burnt and accompanying offerings in both accounts; Samuel additionally names the Lord of hosts.

Both accounts distribute bread to each Israelite, men and women. Chronicles specifies one baker’s loaf and a cake; Samuel lists a loaf, a hearth cake, and a frying-pan flat cake, so the food lists are not collapsed.
The Levites’ appointed ministry of sounding, thanksgiving, and praise before the ark is the kind of instrumental tent ministry earlier described as established by David when the ark came to rest.

Asaph and the listed musicians fill out the Levites whom David has just appointed to sound, give thanks, and praise before the ark; the cymbals, harps, and lyres specify how that commissioned ministry is performed.
Asaph’s cymbal duty before the settled ark continues the specific instrument assignment made to him with Aiman and Aithan in the procession.
Banaias and Oziel are explicitly priests sounding trumpets before the ark, matching the legal assignment of trumpet blowing to Aaron’s sons rather than to the whole congregation.
David’s appointment of praise through Asaph and his brethren introduces the following calls to give thanks, sing, recount wonders, and seek the Lord, identifying the content of the commissioned song.
Both openings call for thanksgiving to the Lord, invocation of His name, and proclamation of His works among peoples or nations.
Both verses pair singing or music to God with recounting His wonders; Chronicles expands the recounting to everyone and explicitly calls them the Lord’s deeds.
Both join praise in God’s holy name to the rejoicing heart of the seeker; Chronicles speaks of seeking His good pleasure, while the psalm speaks of seeking the Lord.
The commands to seek the Lord, be strengthened, and seek His face continually occur together in both verses.
Both call hearers to remember God’s wonders, His portents, and the judgments of His mouth in the same threefold sequence.
Both address the servants and Jacob’s chosen sons, but Chronicles says offspring of Israel whereas the psalm says offspring of Abraham; the shared address does not erase that difference.
Both confess that He is the Lord our God and extend His judgments throughout the earth.
Both connect God’s enduring remembrance of His covenant with His commanded word for a thousand generations; the source says remembers and the psalm remembered.
The song’s enduring covenant recollection is grounded in the narrated covenant with Abram promising land to his seed; the following song verses identify Abraham and Canaan explicitly.
Both specify the covenant with Abraham and the oath to Isaac as the patriarchal commitments remembered by God.
The song links the covenant with Abraham and God’s oath to Isaac; God’s promise to Isaac in Genesis explicitly establishes the oath sworn to Abraham and promises the land to Isaac and his seed.
Both describe the promise established for Jacob as an ordinance and for Israel as an everlasting covenant.
The covenant established for Jacob is illustrated by God’s direct promise to Jacob of land, seed, protection, and eventual return, with Abraham and Isaac explicitly named.
Both quote the divine gift of Canaan as the measured allotment or portion of the recipients’ inheritance.
The song’s gift of Canaan as inheritance corresponds to the covenant’s land promise to Abram’s seed and its list of peoples including the Canaanites; the boundary detail belongs to Genesis alone.
Both place the land promise in the time when its recipients were few and living there as strangers or sojourners.
The song recalls the promise recipients living as strangers in the land; God likewise tells Isaac to live as a stranger there while promising that land to him and his seed.
Both describe the patriarchal travelers passing from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people.
Both say God prevented others from overpowering or wronging the travelers and rebuked kings on their behalf.

God’s protection of the patriarchs by reproving kings is concretely illustrated by His warning to Abimelech to return Abraham’s wife and by His statement that He had restrained the king from touching her.
The same paired prohibitions protect God’s anointed ones from being touched and His prophets from wicked treatment.

The prohibition against harming God’s prophets has a specific patriarchal parallel when God identifies Abraham as a prophet and warns the king to restore his wife; Genesis does not call Abraham anointed here.
Chronicles combines the summons for all the earth to sing with daily proclamation of salvation; these appear across the first two verses of this psalm.
Both give the Lord’s greatness, worthiness of praise, and fearsome supremacy above the gods as reasons for worship.
Both contrast the nations’ gods with the Lord as maker of heaven, while Chronicles calls those gods idols and the psalm calls them demons.

Both describe what stands before God and what characterizes His holy place, but preserve their distinct pairs: glory and praise, strength and boasting in Chronicles; thanksgiving and beauty, holiness and magnificence in the psalm.
Both summon the families of the nations to give or bring the Lord glory; Chronicles pairs glory with strength, while the psalm pairs it with honor.
Both call for glory to God’s name, bringing gifts or sacrifices, and worship in His holy courts; Chronicles gathers into one verse what the psalm spreads over two.
Chronicles combines the earth’s fear before God with its being set right and unshaken; the psalm joins the earth’s shaking before Him to the inhabited world’s establishment so it will not be shaken.
The proclamation among nations that the Lord reigns and the rejoicing of heaven and earth occur together in Chronicles and across these two psalm verses.
Both extend cosmic praise from the sea and its fullness to the land and what fills it; Chronicles specifically says the tree of the field, while the psalm says the plains.
Both give the forest trees joy before the Lord because He comes to judge the earth; the psalm further characterizes that judgment by righteousness and truth.
Both call for thanksgiving and confess mercy enduring for ever; Chronicles says for it is good, whereas the psalm explicitly says He is good.
Both petition God for salvation and rescue or gathering from the nations, with the purpose of praising His holy name and glorying or boasting in His praise.
Both bless the Lord, Israel’s God, from age to age and call for the people’s assent. Chronicles uses Amen and adds their praise; the psalm repeats May it be.
Leaving Asaph and his brethren to perform each day’s ministry carries forward David’s earlier appointment of Levites under Asaph for praise before the ark.
Asaph’s continuing daily ministry before the ark belongs to the tent-based musical service which the earlier summary says David appointed and which continued until Solomon built the house.

The phrase with Abdedom and his brethren extends the group left at the ark for daily ministry, then specifically assigns Abdedom son of Idithon and Ossa as gatekeepers; the preceding verse supplies the personnel list’s governing action.

Sadok and his brother priests remain before the Lord’s tent at Gabaon; the later account locates Moses’ Tent of Testimony and the bronze altar at Gabaon while distinguishing the ark’s tent in Jerusalem.
The continuous burnt offerings morning and evening under Moses’ law correspond to Numbers’ prescription of daily lambs, one in the morning and the second toward evening, as a continual whole burning.
Both descriptions bind priestly altar service to Moses’ commands; the source specifies continual morning and evening burnt offerings, while the earlier summary also includes incense and atonement.
The chosen singers are assigned to praise the Lord because His mercy endures for ever, repeating the stated refrain of thanksgiving in the song just supplied.
The trumpets, cymbals, and song instruments equip the named and chosen praise ministry just listed, while the final clause distinguishes Idithon’s sons’ duty at the gate.
Both accounts close the public celebration with the people returning to their houses and David returning to bless his household; Samuel then continues with the household confrontation.

David contrasts his cedar house with the ark’s temporary shelter before Nathan in both accounts; Chronicles says beneath skins, while Samuel calls it the tent and adds possession on every side away from surrounding enemies.

Stephen’s account places the wilderness tent before David’s request for a dwelling and Solomon’s building; it follows the same movement from David’s concern about the ark’s shelter to a house built by his successor.
Nathan initially authorizes David to do what is in his soul or heart because God is with him, before the following nocturnal revelation redirects the project.
Both accounts mark the divine word to Nathan as arriving that night, introducing the correction to his earlier approval.
Both divine speeches send Nathan to David as God’s servant and explicitly say that David will not build the house for God to dwell in.
David later recalls the prohibition against his building the house and identifies Solomon as the son who will build it, adding warfare and bloodshed as the reason for the prohibition.
Both explain the refusal by recalling God’s movement in a tent and lodging since bringing Israel up; Samuel explicitly names the departure from Egypt.
God’s recalled movement with Israel in a tent corresponds to Stephen’s summary of the Tent of Testimony passing from the wilderness through Joshua’s generation until David’s days.
Both ask whether God ever demanded a cedar house from an Israelite tribe commissioned to shepherd His people during His movement among them.
Both divine speeches identify David’s elevation from the sheepfold to leadership over Israel as God’s own action.
The psalm likewise says God chose David from the sheep flocks to shepherd Jacob and Israel, expanding the transition from literal shepherding to rule over the people.
Both recount God’s presence with David, destruction of his enemies, and grant of a name among the earth’s great ones.

The oracle’s presence with David and defeat of his enemies correspond to the psalm’s named David, divine support, defeat of enemies, and abiding mercy; neither passage reduces his success to independent power.
Both promise to plant Israel in a place of its own where anxiety and renewed oppression by injustice will cease.
Both refer to the judges, enemies, and a house promise, but the supplied texts differ: Chronicles says the Lord will build David a house, while this Samuel verse says David will build Him a house.
The later prayer explicitly interprets the house promise as God’s disclosure that He would build David a house, confirming the beneficiary and builder in the earlier oracle.
Both promise that after David sleeps with his fathers, God will raise up bodily offspring after him and establish that offspring’s kingdom.
The promise of an offspring’s kingdom is later specified as God’s choice of Solomon from David’s sons to sit on the throne; that later speech also states a condition of continued obedience.
Both assign building the divine house to David’s successor and promise an enduring throne; Samuel explicitly says a house for God’s name.
The later speech explicitly names Solomon and repeats that he will build the house and that God will establish his kingdom’s throne for ever.
Both promise a father-son relationship and mercy not withdrawn as previously; Samuel additionally includes correction for wrongdoing, which this Chronicles verse does not include.

Hebrews uses the same Father-to-him and Son-to-Me formula in its argument about the Son’s superiority to angels; this is a later christological use of the royal-sonship wording, not an assertion that the entire immediate building oracle concerns only that later setting.
Both promise lasting security and an established throne, but Chronicles locates the successor in My house and in his kingdom, while Samuel says his house and his kingdom before Me.
The promise of an enduring royal throne is taken up in Gabriel’s announcement of Jesus, who receives David’s throne and whose kingdom has no end; Luke explicitly names the later recipient.
Both close the revelation by affirming that Nathan reported all its words and the whole vision to David.
David sits before the Lord and asks who he and his house are to receive such love; Chronicles says for ever, while Samuel says to this extent.
David’s question Who am I in response to favor for his house recurs in his later thanksgiving over the people’s offerings, where he attributes their ability and gifts to God.
Both move from the present favor to a far-future word about David’s house; Chronicles describes a human vision and exaltation, while Samuel says the law of the human being.
David asks what more he can say and appeals to God’s knowledge of His servant in both prayers; Chronicles explicitly frames the additional speech as giving glory.
Both attribute God’s great action to His own heart; Samuel additionally grounds it in His word and says it was made known to His servant.
Both confess that none is like the Lord and no other God exists, grounding the confession in what the speakers have heard.
David’s confession that no God is besides the Lord echoes Deuteronomy’s conclusion from Israel’s heard revelation and deliverance that the Lord alone is God in heaven and earth.
Both distinguish Israel as the people God redeemed from Egypt for Himself, connecting that redemption, His great name, and the removal of nations before them.
Both passages emphasize the extraordinary act of God taking a people for Himself from Egypt and driving nations out before them, linking Israel’s distinct status to His redeeming action.
Both prayer verses affirm Israel as God’s people for ever and the Lord as their God.
David asks God to confirm for ever the word spoken concerning His servant and the servant’s house in both prayers.

David’s request that the word about his house stand for ever directly answers the oracle’s promises of a successor, a kingdom, and an enduring throne; the prayer seeks enactment of the specific preceding promise.

Both prayers invoke the Lord Almighty, God of Israel, in connection with His word about David’s house; Chronicles asks that the house stand upright, while Samuel asks confirmation of the word and magnification of God’s name.
Both prayers say God disclosed to His servant that He would build him a house, and that this revelation gave David the courage or heart to pray.
Both confess that the Lord is God and has spoken good things concerning His servant; Samuel also expressly calls His words true.
Both conclude by asking that God’s blessing keep David’s house before Him for ever; Chronicles says He has begun to bless, while Samuel petitions Him now to begin.
David’s plea for his house to remain blessed for ever corresponds to the psalm’s enduring mercy and covenant for David, lasting seed and throne, and refusal to revoke the pledged word.
Both campaign summaries begin with David striking and routing the foreigners and taking territory; Chronicles specifies Geth and its villages while Samuel says the separated territory.
Both report David striking Moab and Moab becoming his servants bringing gifts; Samuel additionally narrates measured groups put to death or kept alive, which Chronicles does not state.
Both place David’s strike against the northern king in an attempt to establish control at the Euphrates. Chronicles names Adraazar of Souba and Hemath; Samuel names Hadadezer son of Raab of Zobah.

Both give one thousand chariots, seven thousand in the mounted category, twenty thousand foot soldiers, and a hundred chariots retained after disabling the rest; Chronicles says horses where Samuel says horsemen.

David disables captured chariots while retaining a hundred; Joshua’s earlier victory includes God’s command to hamstring enemy horses and burn chariots. The related removal of captured military transport does not make the methods or retained quantity identical.
Both describe help coming from Damascus to the opposing king and David striking twenty-two thousand Syrians; the king’s forms remain Adraazar in Chronicles and Hadadezer in Samuel.
Both combine a garrison near Damascus, Syrian service and gifts, and the attribution of David’s recurring deliverance or victory to the Lord.
Both place golden objects taken from the opposing king’s servants in Jerusalem. Chronicles calls them collars and Samuel armlets; Samuel additionally supplies a later Egyptian removal notice.
Both connect the great quantity of captured bronze to Solomon’s bronze sea, pillars, and vessels. Chronicles names Metabechas and Samuel Masbak; Samuel additionally lists basins.

The source identifies captured bronze as material for Solomon’s sea; the later construction account describes that cast sea and its form, connecting material provision with the named temple furnishing.

Both introduce the king of the northern city hearing of David’s defeat of his enemy’s whole force, opening the congratulatory embassy; the forms are Thoa/Hemath/Adraazar and Toi/Hamath/Hadadezer respectively.

Both describe the king sending his son to inquire after David’s peace and bless him for defeating a common opponent. Chronicles names Idouram and silver and gold vessels; Samuel names Ieddouran and also bronze vessels.
Both dedicate the acquired precious metals to the Lord and list Idumea, Moab, Ammon, the foreigners, and Amalek; Samuel also explicitly includes the northern king’s spoil.

David consecrates silver and gold taken from the nations; the later treasury notice explicitly includes holy things consecrated by David and gifts taken from wars and spoils for the building of God’s house. It does not identify every item in this campaign list individually.

Both notices give eighteen thousand struck in Idumea, but Chronicles credits Abessa son of Sarouia at the Valley of Salts, while Samuel credits David and names Gaimale; the differing actor and location wording are retained.
Both follow the Idumean victory with garrisons, Idumean subjection, and the Lord’s repeated deliverance of David; Chronicles places garrisons in the valley, Samuel throughout Idumea.
Both reign summaries explicitly join David’s rule over Israel to administering judgment and righteousness for all his people.
David’s administration of judgment and righteousness gives royal content to the psalm’s picture of him chosen from the flocks to shepherd Israel with an innocent heart and understanding hands.

Both administration lists put Joab over the army and pair him with an officer over records. Chronicles calls the recorder Josaphat son of Achiloud, Samuel Jehoshaphat son of Ahia; the different patronymics are preserved.

Both lists name the two priestly lines and a writing officer; Chronicles gives Sadok, Achimelech, and Sousa, whereas Samuel gives Zadok, Ahimelech, and Asa. The parallel offices do not establish an independent name equivalence for the secretary.

Both closing administration entries mention the Cherethite/Pelethite groups and David’s sons, but Chronicles puts Banaias over those groups and calls the sons foremost successors; Samuel calls Benaiah counselor and the sons palace officials.
Both narratives open with the Ammonite king’s death and succession by his son; Chronicles names Naas and Anan, while Samuel names the successor Hanun in this verse.

Both ground David’s condolence mission in reciprocating the deceased father’s mercy and send servants to comfort the new Ammonite king; each account retains its own forms of the father’s and son’s names.
In both accounts Ammon’s leaders reinterpret David’s comforters as spies searching the city; Chronicles also explicitly names spying out the land.
Both describe the new king humiliating David’s servants by shaving and cutting away half their cloaks before dismissing them; Chronicles says up to the fold, Samuel at their hips.
Both have David respond to the messengers’ dishonor by sending to meet them and instructing them to remain in Jericho until their beards grow.

Both follow the messengers’ shaming with Ammon hiring Syrian aid. Chronicles specifies a thousand talents and chariots and horsemen from its named regions; Samuel lists twenty thousand foot soldiers and additional numbered groups of men, with different regional wording.

Both describe the hired forces assembling separately from Ammon, but Chronicles gives thirty-two thousand chariots and Maidaba, while Samuel gives several manpower contingents and says the allied forces were in the field.
David responds to the report by sending Joab with the whole force of mighty men in both narratives.
Both separate Ammon’s formation at the city gate from the allied forces in the open field or plain; Samuel names the allied regions individually.
Joab recognizes fighting in front and behind and selects Israelite young men to face Syria in both accounts, explaining the division of his force.
Both entrust the remaining troops to Joab’s brother to face Ammon, with the brother named Abessa in Chronicles and Abishai in Samuel.
Both speeches arrange reciprocal rescue: the force facing Syria will receive help if overmatched, and it will help the force facing Ammon if needed.
Both exhort courage for the people and God’s cities and entrust the outcome to what the Lord judges good in His eyes.

Joab’s acceptance that the Lord will do what is good in His eyes echoes Eli’s acceptance of the Lord’s announced judgment. The common submission formula is applied to military uncertainty in Chronicles and prophetic judgment in Samuel.
Both describe Joab and his accompanying troops moving into battle against Syria and the Syrian force fleeing before him.
Ammon flees into the city after seeing Syria flee, and Joab returns to Jerusalem in both accounts. Chronicles names both Joab and Abessa in the flight, whereas Samuel names Abishai there.
Both describe a Syrian regrouping and forces summoned from beyond the River under a commander. Chronicles names Sophach and Adraazar; Samuel names Shobach and Hadadezer and adds Chalamak and Ailam.
David gathers all Israel, crosses the Jordan, and faces the Syrian battle line in both accounts; Samuel additionally names Ailam as the destination.

Both report Syrian flight and the commander’s death, but Chronicles gives seven thousand chariot fighters and forty thousand foot soldiers, while Samuel gives seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen; the figures and troop types remain distinct.

Both close with the defeated ruler’s dependents submitting and Syria ceasing to aid Ammon. Chronicles specifies a covenant with David and service to him; Samuel describes desertion to Israel and fear of further help.
